speaker_role: test-prep/consultancy marketer (Rob Franek, editor-in-chief, The Princeton Review)
commercial_incentive: Promotes Princeton Review website/tools and its Q&A series
key_insights: Early Decision is binding: apply to only one school, must attend if accepted, can't reapply to that school same year if rejected but can go elsewhere if deferred or rejected
Some schools offer a second Early Decision round (ED2) with a January deadline and February decision
Early Action is non-binding and lets you apply to multiple colleges, except some selective schools cap it via 'single-choice/restrictive' early action limiting you to one school
Regular decision deadlines are typically January/February with March/April decisions; ED deadlines run October 15-November 15 with December decisions
Applying early can sometimes improve acceptance odds at certain colleges, per Princeton Review's published early-vs-regular acceptance-rate data

Biggest ED downside is financial: admitted ED students must accept whatever aid package is offered with no ability to compare against other schools' offers, and may miss out on other scholarship opportunities
EA preserves the ability to compare financial aid and scholarship offers across schools before committing
specific_numbers_or_facts: ED deadlines usually November 1 or 15, some as early as October 15 (Rob Franek/Princeton Review)
ED decisions typically returned in December; regular decisions in March/April (Princeton Review)
ED2 deadline in January with decision in February (Princeton Review)
notable_or_distinctive: Clearly separates ED2 as a distinct cycle and flags single-choice/restrictive early action as a lesser-known EA variant, but otherwise generic overview.
